en: I worship the state of Vāsudeva, which is the chamber of the heart of all, wherein everything is established,
yet which in reality is without any support.

Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and likewise strength and all the senses swell with vigor. May everything be the Upaniṣad of Brahman. May I not repudiate Brahman, and may Brahman not repudiate me. May there be no repudiation; may there be non-repudiation for me. Those duties which are found in the Upaniṣads belong to one who is devoted to the Self.
May they be with me; may they be with me. Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ. Having paid homage to Vāsudeva, the Lord of all, the blessed Nārada asked:

"Teach me, O Blessed One; tell me the procedure for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), together with its materials, mantras, and proper locations. To him, the blessed Vāsudeva replied: "[It is] produced from the station of Vaikuṇṭha..."

This Viṣṇucandana, which brings me joy and is worn by my devotees beginning with Brahmā, was daily smeared upon my body by the Gopīs; because it was washed off [by them], it became known as Gopīcandana. This meritorious ointment from my body, situated within Cakratīrtha, marked with the discus, yellow in color, and the means to liberation, is thus described.
Then, having prostrated to and taken up the gopīcandana:
"O gopīcandana, destroyer of sins, born from the body of Viṣṇu!
O you who are marked with the discus, salutations to you; be the bestower of liberation through your wearing."
Taking water with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," he should rub it with "viṣṇornukaṃ.

Then, with the mantras "ato devā avantu naḥ" and the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, or with the names beginning with Keśava, he should apply [the clay]. A student (brahmacārī) or a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should apply it on the forehead, heart, throat, and the roots of the upper arms using the Vaiṣṇava-gāyatrī.

Or one may wear it while reciting the names beginning with Kṛṣṇa. Having consecrated it three times in this manner, one should meditate thus: "O Acyuta, whose hands hold the conch, discus, and mace; O dweller of Dvārakā; O Govinda, lotus-eyed one, protect me who have come to you for refuge."
A householder should apply [the mark] on twelve places, such as the forehead and others, using the ring finger, either with the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī or with the names beginning with Keśava.
A student (brahmacārī) or a householder should apply it on the forehead, heart, throat, and the roots of the arms.
One should apply [the marks] with the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī or with the names beginning with Kṛṣṇa.
A *yati* (ascetic) should apply them on the head, forehead, and heart with the *praṇava* alone.
The three forms are Brahmā and the others; the three sacred utterances (*vyāhṛtis*) are the three meters (*chandāṃsi*).

"The three fires" refers to the three luminous times, the three states, and the three selves; the three upward tilakas are the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*. These are the upward tilakas consisting of the *praṇava*; their essence is this very *om*. These [tilakas] are one.
It became even. Because one raises it upwards, it is called *oṃ*;
thus, one should wear the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*). A *paramahaṃsa* should wear a single vertical mark on the forehead with the *praṇava*.
The yogi, beholding his own self as the light that illuminates reality,
attains union with me; or else, [beholding it] either in the center of the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) applied upon the heart or in the center of the lotus of the heart.
In its center, a flame of fire stands upwards, subtler than the subtle;
brilliant like a streak of lightning in the midst of dark clouds,
as slender as the awn of a grain of wild rice, there the Supreme Self is established.
Therefore, one should practice meditation upon Him who resides in the *puṇḍra* within the lotuses of the heart;
in this manner, one should gradually contemplate Me, the Supreme Hari, as one's own Self.
He who meditates with a one-pointed mind upon Me, the imperishable Hari—
And within the lotus of the heart, he realizes his own self; of this there is no doubt that he is liberated.
Through devotion, he knows my form—the non-dual Brahman, devoid of beginning, middle, or end, self-luminous, existence-consciousness-bliss, and immutable.
Vishnu is one, though he dwells as the single Self pervading the many— both moving and stationary beings; I am established within all creatures,
just as oil is in sesame seeds, fire is in wood, and ghee is in milk.
Just as fragrance resides in flowers, so do I abide within all beings.

Having smeared oneself with Gopīcandana and meditated there upon Hari, the sun of consciousness, located at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), between the eyebrows, and in the heart, one shall attain the Supreme.
With an upright staff, with vital energy directed upward, with the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, and possessing the upward yoga,
the ascetic who possesses this "fourfold upward" state attains the supreme goal.
This certain knowledge is accomplished of its own accord through devotion to Me.

By wearing *gopīcandana*, one shall possess constant and one-pointed devotion. For all Brāhmaṇas who follow the Vedas, the application of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* with *gopīcandana* paste and water is prescribed as the most excellent practice.
One who desires liberation and seeks the realization of the immediate Self should constantly wear the earth from the root of the *tulasī* plant in the absence of *gopīcandana*.
This [earth] is like the ashes of the *atirātra* and *agnihotra* sacrifices; it is the ash of the fire, [consecrated by] "This is Viṣṇu" and "The three steps."
One should perform the smearing with the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī mantra and the Praṇava.
In this manner, one should wear the Gopīcandana according to the prescribed rite.
Whoever studies [this] becomes purified from all sins.
Evil intent does not arise in him; he becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords; he becomes as one who has performed all sacrifices; he becomes worthy of worship by all the gods;
and there arises in him unwavering devotion toward me, the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained right knowledge, he reaches union with Viṣṇu;
he does not return again, he does not return again—thus said the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. And whoever studies this also becomes exactly like that. Om. Truth. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, as well as strength and all the senses, be nourished. May everything be the Upaniṣad of Brahman. May I not repudiate Brahman; may Brahman not repudiate me. May there be no repudiation; may there be for me no repudiation.
Whatever dharmas are contained in the Upanishads for one intent upon the Self, may those be in me; may they be in me.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Vāsudevopaniṣad.
